Critical Care

Differentiated effect of hypothermia versus normothermia after cardiac arrest by neurological status and clinical correlates of ischemic burden

Lileikyte G, Marinho LL, Lu Y et al. · 2026 Nov 02
Study Type: Secondary analysis of two RCTs (TTM and TTM2) using machine learning (causal forests, BART) to assess heterogeneity of treatment effect.
Key Question: Does the effect of 33 °C versus normothermia after OHCA differ according to ischaemic burden correlates or admission neurological findings?
Key Findings:
  • Among 2789 OHCA patients, six-month mortality was 49.4% (33 °C) versus 47.9% (normothermia).
  • No significant heterogeneity of treatment effect was found across methods or populations. Pooled conditional mortality risk differences ranged from -1.2% to 2.1% (causal forest, p=0.99) and -0.5% to 1.5% (BART); posterior probability of hypothermia benefit was 42–53%.
  • Subgroup estimates and poor functional outcome (mRS 4–6) showed the same pattern.
Clinical Relevance: The findings argue against selecting hypothermia for patients with perceived greater ischaemic injury or worse initial neurology, supporting a pragmatic approach (e.g. fever avoidance/controlled normothermia) in UK post-arrest care rather than targeting 33 °C by phenotype.
Limitations: Heterogeneity analysis was limited to available baseline variables and cannot exclude effect modification by unmeasured factors, and secondary analyses may be underpowered to detect modest subgroup effects.

Intensive Care Medicine

Sodium bicarbonate therapy for metabolic acidosis in critically ill patients: a Bayesian systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials

Kitisin N, Walker HGM, Jung B et al. · 2026 Nov 02
Study Type: Systematic review and Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis of RCTs (4 trials, 1544 patients).
Key Question: Does intravenous sodium bicarbonate improve mortality or renal outcomes in critically ill adults with metabolic acidosis?
Key Findings:
  • Short-term all-cause mortality: no clear benefit (RR 0.94, 95% CrI 0.73–1.22; posterior probability of benefit 72.1%).
  • RRT initiation: lower risk with bicarbonate (RR 0.74, 95% CrI 0.59–0.98; posterior probability of benefit 97.2%).
  • Other secondary outcomes (90-day mortality, RRT-free days, vasopressor-free days, length of stay) were small or imprecise; no consistent safety signal.
Clinical Relevance: Supports considering bicarbonate in selected acidotic patients (e.g. AKI) to reduce RRT use, though it does not justify routine use for survival benefit and does not replace local guidance.
Limitations: Only four trials contributed, so estimates are imprecise and heterogeneity in populations and acidosis severity limits identification of who benefits.

Journal of Critical Care

Impact of the updated SOFA-2 score on organ dysfunction assessment and trial outcomes in Sepsis: A reanalysis of two randomized trials

Leland S, Bank H, Shvilkina T et al. · 2026 Nov 04
Study Type: Secondary (post hoc) reanalysis of two RCT datasets (ACTS and TRPSS) using retrospectively reconstructed SOFA-2 scores.
Key Question: Does rescoring sepsis trial data with SOFA-2 rather than SOFA-1 change organ dysfunction measurement and the interpretation of trial outcomes?
Key Findings:
  • SOFA-2 gave lower total scores than SOFA-1 in both cohorts (ACTS median 9 vs 7; TRPSS 11 vs 10; both p<0.001), driven by lower respiratory and cardiovascular subscores, partly offset by higher coagulation subscores.
  • ACTS primary outcome remained non-significant under SOFA-2 (MD -0.8, 95% CI -1.6 to 0.0, p=0.06), but reached significance in an exploratory post hoc analysis incorporating approximated urine output (MD -0.84, 95% CI -1.64 to -0.05, p=0.04).
  • In TRPSS, SOFA-2 did not change overall interpretation but attenuated the treatment effect at all timepoints.
Clinical Relevance: As SOFA-2 adoption approaches, historical SOFA-based trial results and cohort comparisons may not be directly interchangeable, so score version must be stated when interpreting critical care evidence.
Limitations: SOFA-2 was reconstructed from available data (urine output approximated), and the significant ACTS finding came from a post hoc exploratory analysis, so it should be treated as hypothesis-generating.

Critical Care

Early adequate empiric antifungal therapy and 28-day mortality in ICU patients with candidemia: a pooled patient-level analysis of EUROBACT-1 and EUROBACT-2 cohorts

Wozniak H, Tabah A, Bassetti M et al. · 2026 Oct 16
Study Type: Pooled secondary analysis of two prospective observational cohorts (EUROBACT-1 and -2), with propensity-weighted Cox regression.
Key Question: Is adequate empiric antifungal therapy started within 2 days of blood culture draw associated with lower 28-day mortality in ICU patients with candidemia?
Key Findings:
  • 272 patients from 158 centres; 110 received early adequate therapy, 162 did not. Crude 28-day mortality was 40.9% vs 37.0% respectively.
  • After inverse probability weighting, early adequate therapy was not associated with mortality (HR 1.23, 95% CI 0.82–1.83, p=0.314).
  • Results were consistent across subgroups (cohort, Candida species, hypotension at onset) and in a frailty model accounting for centre effects.
Clinical Relevance: The findings support a more targeted approach to empiric antifungal use, which is relevant to UK antimicrobial stewardship, though they do not justify withholding early therapy in high-risk patients.
Limitations: Observational design with a modest sample size (wide confidence interval compatible with both benefit and harm) and likely residual confounding by indication, so the study cannot exclude a clinically meaningful treatment effect.

Critical Care

Fluid-intolerance signals as bedside safety limits during early septic shock resuscitation: a multicenter randomized trial

Melo P, Amthauer M, Ferri G et al. · 2026 Sep 26
Study Type: Multicentre, open-label RCT (three Chilean ICUs), stopped early for infeasibility.
Key Question: Does limiting fluid boluses using bedside fluid-intolerance signals (lung ultrasound, VExUS, E/e', CVP) during early septic shock resuscitation improve oxygenation without impairing resolution of hypoperfusion?
Key Findings:
  • 35 patients analysed (17 intervention, 18 standard care) against 62 planned. Protocol bolus volume was lower with the intervention (median 250 vs 650 mL; difference −500 mL, 95% CI −750 to −250), but cumulative fluid from pre-randomisation to 6 h was similar (3375 vs 3750 mL).
  • ΔPaO2:FiO2 at 6 h favoured the intervention (+40.5 vs −37.9; median difference +78.3, 95% CI 50.5 to 110.0).
  • Lactate and capillary refill time changes did not differ between groups.
Clinical Relevance: Suggests multimodal ultrasound-guided fluid-intolerance assessment is feasible at the bedside and may limit fluid-related respiratory deterioration, which is relevant to UK practice, where fluid-sparing strategies in sepsis are under active debate.
Limitations: The trial was underpowered and stopped early, was open-label, and used a physiological surrogate (oxygenation) as the primary outcome, so the authors themselves conclude the effect remains uncertain and no patient-centred outcomes can be inferred.

Critical Care

Structural imbalances in open-access critical care research: a bibliometric analysis of abstracts from ICU database studies, 2018-2025

Kokoefer A, Deribe AG, Zimmermann G et al. · 2026 Aug 19
Study Type: Bibliometric analysis (systematic search with semi-automated AI-based data extraction)
Key Question: What is the volume, geographic origin, methodological character and impact of research using six open-access ICU databases (2018–2025)?
Key Findings:
  • 4,648 publications; output rose 45-fold (42 to 1,907/year), accelerating after MIMIC-IV release. MIMIC-IV (54.6%) and MIMIC-III (30.0%) dominated; European databases accounted for 1.9%. China produced 65.6% of papers, the USA 10.6%.
  • Mostly retrospective observational designs (67.9%), focused on mortality prediction in sepsis. Median AUROC 0.798 (1,263 papers); AUROC was not correlated with citations. Median citations were 5.0 per paper.
  • External validation across datasets was rarely evident in abstracts.
Clinical Relevance: Published ML/prediction models derived largely from US-based MIMIC data may not generalise to UK/European practice, so clinicians should scrutinise external validation before considering clinical use.
Limitations: Data extraction relied on abstracts alone via an LLM pipeline (validated on only 110 papers), so methodological details such as external validation may be underreported.

Annals of Intensive Care

Chloride load and serum chloride in critically ill adults: a randomization-anchored analysis of the BaSICS trial

Zampieri FG, Maia IS, Machado FR et al. · 2026
Study Type: Secondary analysis of a multicentre RCT (BaSICS; Bayesian hierarchical longitudinal modelling), restricted to 3,482 patients (33% of trial population) with serum chloride data.
Key Question: How does randomisation to 0.9% saline versus Plasma-Lyte 148 alter early serum chloride, and how much of the variation in chloride is attributable to fluid choice?
Key Findings:
  • By day 2, serum chloride rose 2.15 mmol/L more with saline (95% CI 1.76-2.53), equating to 1.47 mmol/L per 100 mmol additional chloride; the difference was larger with lower baseline eGFR (+3.0 mmol/L at eGFR 30 vs +1.8 at 90).
  • Fluid accounted for only 0.7% of modelled chloride variation (1.8% including randomised arm); baseline characteristics, mainly baseline chloride, explained 48.1%, with the remainder reflecting patient-specific differences and day-to-day fluctuation.
Clinical Relevance: Saline-related hyperchloraemia is modest and largely driven by baseline chloride and renal function, which may temper chloride-focused fluid strategies in UK ICUs, though patients with reduced eGFR show the greatest effect.
Limitations: Only a third of trial patients were analysed, with measurement attrition over time, and the volume-chloride association is observational and open to residual confounding.

Annals of Intensive Care

Sex differences in limitations of life-sustaining treatment in the intensive care unit: A nationwide cohort study

Hägglöf E, Eriksson J, Bell M et al. · 2026
Study Type: Nationwide registry-based cohort study (Swedish Intensive Care Register, 2019–2024).
Key Question: Does the likelihood, timing and documented rationale for limitation of life-sustaining treatment (LST) in ICU differ between women and men?
Key Findings:
  • Among 111,354 adults, LST-limitations were more frequent in women (25.3% vs 23.8%); adjusted for SAPS3 and age, OR 1.21 (95% CI 1.17–1.25), and OR 1.24 (1.18–1.32) among 30-day non-survivors.
  • Limitations were set earlier in women (median 2.8 h vs 4.5 h after admission).
  • Documented reasons differed: acute disease and therapy failure more common in men; autonomy and chronic disease more common in women. Patient involvement was documented more often in women (13.3% vs 11.8%).
Clinical Relevance: Suggests sex-related variation in end-of-life decision-making that UK units may wish to audit, particularly the timing and documentation of ceilings of treatment and escalation decisions.
Limitations: Observational registry data cannot establish whether differences reflect appropriate individualisation or bias, and they rely on documented rather than actual reasoning, with residual confounding (e.g. frailty, comorbidity, patient preferences) likely.
